cultivar: Large-leaf assamica-type old tea trees, seed-grown, many claimed to be several centuries old
processing: Made like raw pu-erh: wilted, wok-fired to kill green, hand-rolled and sun-dried into maocha, then either sold loose or steamed and pressed into cakes; traditional village tea was also packed into bamboo tubes, and some lots carry a smokiness from wood-fired woks.
harvest_season: Spring (March to April) is the main and best harvest and the one usually pressed; a smaller autumn pick gives softer, cheaper tea.
appearance_dry: Large, thick, grey-green to dark olive leaves with silvery buds, pressed into loosely bound cakes or sold as long twisted loose leaf, smelling of honey, hay and sometimes wood smoke.
appearance_liquor: Pale gold when young, amber with age, clear and oily.
appearance_wet: Big leathery leaves and whole buds, yellow-green to olive, with thick stems.
taste_profile: Sweet and thick: honey, dried flowers and a stone-fruit note, a firm but clean bitterness, sometimes a wisp of smoke, and a long cooling sweetness in the throat; aged lots turn towards dried fruit and wood.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, then short steeps with just-boiled water; it is usually less harsh than young Yunnan sheng and can be pushed. Smoky village lots mellow a lot with a year of airing.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year, mostly as young cakes or loose maocha from the last few years, through a few Lao cooperatives and foreign specialists; wrappers name the village (Ban Komaen is the famous one), the year and often the claimed tree age. Cakes are bought to drink young or to age at home; older Lao cakes exist but are scarce, since most old-tree leaf historically went to Chinese buyers and was pressed in Yunnan.
description:
Phongsaly is the northern tip of Laos, a finger of mountains pushed up between Yunnan and Vietnam, and it is known for its old tea trees. The village of Ban Komaen above the provincial capital is the famous one: tall, seed-grown tea trees that the Phunoy villagers say are centuries old, growing in groves rather than rows, picked from ladders. The same kind of old tea grows in Oudomxay and on the Xieng Khouang plateau further south.

Much of this tea is said to have gone to China, loose or packed into bamboo tubes, and some of it is said to come back to the market as 'Yunnan' pu-erh, though nobody has good figures. What has changed more recently is that Lao cooperatives and a few foreign tea companies now process and press it under its own name, in the raw pu-erh manner: wok kill-green, rolling, sun-drying and pressing into cakes.

The tea tastes like what it is, an old-tree assamica sheng from the far southern end of the pu-erh belt. Young, it is honeyed and floral with a stone-fruit note, a thick texture, a firm clean bitterness and a long sweet aftertaste; many village lots carry a little wood smoke from the firing, which fades with a year of airing. It is usually gentler than young Yunnan sheng. Brew it gongfu style with a rinse and short steeps and expect eight or ten rounds.

It is sold by year and village, as cakes or loose maocha, and almost all of it is young. Prices are below equivalent Yunnan old-tree tea, often well below. Tree-age claims are unverifiable; thick, large leaves, fat buds, a heavy honey sweetness and a lasting aftertaste are the real evidence. Lao tea with no village or year on it is usually plantation leaf from the Bolaven Plateau in the south, a different and more ordinary product.

If you drink Yunnan sheng, Phongsaly is the obvious comparison: the same tree lineage, a few valleys away, with its own softer, sweeter accent.
sources_note: No Lao-script name given (the generic Lao word for tea is 'saa'; a specific native product name is not established). Tree ages at Ban Komaen (often quoted as 400+ years) are local claims. The share of Lao leaf sold into Yunnan is widely reported in the tea trade but unquantified. Category 'sheng' chosen because the product is made and sold as raw pu-erh style; 'Pu'er tea' would be the alternative umbrella article.
history:
Phongsaly is the far north of Laos, wedged between Yunnan and Vietnam, and its old tea trees belong to the same broad tea country as southern Yunnan. Little is documented about when they were planted. The villagers around Ban Komaen say their trees are centuries old, and that remains a local claim rather than a measured age.

The tea is usually described as long having gone to Chinese buyers, with Lao-labelled raw pu-erh style cakes being the newer development. Dates and volumes for either are hard to pin down.
